course.title: Introduction to Business
course.description: A plain-language tour of how businesses are built, owned, and run, from the corner shop to the global firm. You will meet the forms of ownership, the functional areas, markets and money, ethics, and the stakeholder view that ties them together. Structure informed by the Business entry on Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: What is the most basic purpose of a business?
options: to create value by offering goods or services people are willing to pay for
to employ as many people as possible
to keep cash sitting in a bank account
questions.explanation: A business exists to create and deliver value that customers will pay for - see 'What a business is and its purpose'.

questions.prompt: In which form of ownership are the owner and the business legally the same person, with unlimited personal liability?
questions.explanation: A sole proprietorship has no legal separation, so the owner is personally liable for all debts.

questions.prompt: Which function is responsible for finding customers and communicating the value of a product?
questions.explanation: Marketing identifies needs and communicates value; operations makes the product and accounting records the money.

questions.prompt: If demand for a product rises while supply stays the same, what usually happens to its price?
questions.explanation: More buyers chasing the same quantity pushes the market price up - basic supply and demand.

options: the total money a business takes in
the amount of cash in the till
questions.explanation: Profit is what remains after you subtract all costs from revenue.

questions.prompt: Corporate social responsibility mainly refers to...
options: a company acting in the interests of society and the environment, not only its owners
a legal requirement to double profit every year
a rule that firms must stay small
questions.explanation: Corporate social responsibility is a firm taking responsibility for its wider impact on people and the planet.

questions.prompt: A business plan is most useful because it...
options: sets out the idea, market, operations, and finances before risking money
is required to open a bank account only
questions.explanation: A plan forces an entrepreneur to think through the idea, the market, and the numbers before committing resources.

questions.prompt: Which group is a stakeholder of a business?
options: customers, employees, suppliers, communities, and owners
questions.explanation: Stakeholders are all the groups affected by a firm, not just the people who own shares.

lessons.title: What a business is and its purpose
lessons.grammar_note: Use 'goods' for physical products you can touch and 'services' for work done for someone; many firms sell a mix of both.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what a business actually is, describe why one exists, and name the main groups it serves. By the end you should be able to tell a classmate, in a single clear sentence, what separates a business from a hobby or a charity, and give two reasons firms are created in the first place. You should also be able to spot the difference between goods and services in everyday life and say who benefits from an exchange. Warm-up: think about the last thing you paid for today. Who made it or provided it, what did you hand over, and what did they get in return for giving it to you? Hold that small exchange in mind - it is the seed of every business, from a single market stall up to a company that sells to millions of people across the world.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A business is an organization that creates value by making goods or providing services and offering them in exchange for money. The purpose is not simply to collect cash; it is to meet a need well enough that customers choose to pay. When a baker turns flour, time, and skill into bread that a family wants, the baker has created value - the bread is worth more to the buyer than the coins they give up, and the coins are worth more to the baker than one more loaf on the shelf. Both sides gain, which is why voluntary trade tends to repeat. Most businesses aim to earn a profit, meaning they take in more than they spend, so the owner is rewarded and the firm can keep going. A business is not the same as a charity, which pursues a social mission, or a hobby, which need not pay its own way. The common thread is value created for someone willing to pay for it.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Value is the heart of the matter: a firm thrives only when what it offers is worth more to the customer than the price. Consider three examples. A coffee shop sells a service and a good together - a drink plus a warm place to sit - and survives because regulars find that bundle worth the cost. A software company sells a service delivered over the internet, charging a monthly fee for a tool that saves customers time. A farm sells goods, raw produce, often to other businesses rather than directly to you. In each case the firm must cover its costs, from ingredients and wages to rent and equipment, and still have something left over. Businesses also serve many groups at once, called stakeholders: customers who buy, employees who work, suppliers who sell inputs, owners who invest, and the wider community that is affected. A firm that ignores any of these for too long usually runs into trouble, because each group can walk away.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In one sentence, what is the purpose of a business? 2) Name one good and one service you used this week. 3) Is a volunteer food bank a business? Why or why not? 4) Give two stakeholders of your local bakery. 5) Why does a voluntary trade usually leave both sides better off? Answers: 1) To create value by offering goods or services that customers are willing to pay for. 2) Example: a bus ticket is a service, a sandwich is a good. 3) No - it pursues a social mission and does not sell its output for a profit, though it is still an organization. 4) Customers and employees (also suppliers, owners, the neighborhood). 5) Each side values what it receives more than what it gives up, so both gain from the exchange.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking a business exists only to make money. Money is the result of creating value, not the starting point; firms that chase cash while ignoring customer needs rarely last. Mistake: confusing revenue with profit. Taking in a lot of money means nothing if costs are even higher. Mistake: assuming only owners matter. Employees, suppliers, and the community all shape whether a firm succeeds. Exit ticket: (a) What single thing must a business create to survive? (b) Name two groups, besides owners, that count as stakeholders. Answers: (a) value that customers will pay for; (b) any two of customers, employees, suppliers, and the surrounding community.

lessons.title: Forms of business ownership
lessons.grammar_note: 'Liability' means legal responsibility for debts; 'limited liability' means an owner can lose only what they invested, not their personal home or savings.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the four common forms of business ownership - sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, and limited liability company - and explain the trade-offs between them. By the end you should be able to match a situation to a sensible ownership form and say, in plain terms, what liability and double taxation mean for an owner. Warm-up: imagine you and a friend want to open a small bakery. Who owns it, who is responsible if it cannot pay a supplier, and what happens to any profit at the end of the year? Keep that bakery in mind as a running example, because the right legal form changes the answers to all three of those questions in ways that matter a great deal once real money and real risk are involved.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The legal form of a business decides who owns it, who is responsible for its debts, how it is taxed, and how easily it can raise money. A sole proprietorship is one person who is the business; it is simple to start, but the owner has unlimited liability, meaning personal assets are at risk. A partnership is two or more people sharing ownership, profit, and, in the general form, liability. A corporation is a separate legal person, owned by shareholders, that can enter contracts and be sued in its own name; owners enjoy limited liability, but profits can be taxed twice, once at the company level and again when paid out as dividends. A limited liability company, often written as LLC, blends features of both: owners get limited liability like a corporation while profits can pass straight to owners and be taxed once, like a partnership. Each form trades simplicity against protection and the ability to grow.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Picture the same bakery under each form. As a sole proprietorship, you alone own it; setup is cheap and you keep all profit, but if the oven supplier is unpaid, your personal savings can be seized. As a general partnership with your friend, you split profit and decisions, yet each partner can be held responsible for the whole debt. Turn the bakery into a corporation and it becomes its own legal entity: you and your friend hold shares, your personal homes are shielded, and you can sell more shares to raise cash for a second location - but you face more paperwork and the risk of double taxation on profit. Form it as a limited liability company and you keep the liability shield while profit flows through to you both and is taxed once. Large, fast-growing firms usually become corporations because they can raise money by selling shares; small, local firms often stay sole proprietorships or limited liability companies for simplicity and lighter tax.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which form leaves the owner personally responsible for all business debts? 2) What does limited liability protect? 3) What is double taxation, and which form is most associated with it? 4) Why might a fast-growing firm choose to become a corporation? 5) Which form blends limited liability with pass-through, single taxation? Answers: 1) A sole proprietorship (and a general partnership, for each partner). 2) An owner's personal assets - they can lose only what they put in. 3) Profit taxed once at the company level and again when paid to owners as dividends; it is most associated with the corporation. 4) It can raise money by selling shares to many investors. 5) A limited liability company (LLC).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming a corporation is always best. The extra paperwork, cost, and possible double taxation can outweigh the benefits for a tiny local shop. Mistake: believing a partnership protects each partner. In a general partnership, one partner's debt can fall on the others. Mistake: mixing up the LLC and the corporation - both give limited liability, but they are taxed differently and set up differently. Exit ticket: (a) Which two forms give owners limited liability? (b) Which single-owner form is simplest to start but riskiest for personal assets? Answers: (a) the corporation and the limited liability company; (b) the sole proprietorship.

lessons.title: The functional areas of a business
lessons.grammar_note: A 'function' here means a department or area of work, such as marketing or finance - not a mathematical function.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the main functional areas of a business - management, marketing, operations, finance, accounting, and human resources - and say what each one does. By the end you should be able to take a real task, such as hiring a new worker or launching a product, and point to the function that owns it. Warm-up: think of a company you know well and list every different kind of job it must contain for a single item to reach a customer. Someone has to decide what to make, make it, sell it, pay for it, count the money, and hire the people who do all of that. Those clusters of related work are exactly the functional areas, and understanding them is the fastest way to see how any firm hangs together as a whole.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Even a small firm must do several different kinds of work, and businesses group that work into functional areas. Management sets direction, makes decisions, and coordinates the other areas so they pull together. Marketing studies what customers need, shapes the product and its price, and communicates its value to the right people. Operations is the engine room: it turns inputs into the actual goods or services, managing quality, cost, and timing. Finance decides how to raise money and where to invest it, balancing risk against return. Accounting records every transaction and produces the reports that tell owners and outsiders how the firm is doing. Human resources, often written as HR, recruits, trains, pays, and supports the people who do all the work. These areas overlap and depend on one another; a decision in one ripples into the others, which is why management exists to keep them aligned toward the same goals.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Follow a single new smartphone through the functions. Management decides the firm should enter the phone market and sets a budget. Marketing researches what buyers want, settles on features and a price, and plans the launch campaign. Operations sources parts, runs the factory, and ships finished units on schedule and to standard. Finance arranges the money to pay for tooling and decides whether to borrow or use the firm's own cash. Accounting tracks the spending and the sales, then reports the profit or loss. Human resources hires the engineers and the factory staff, trains them, and handles their pay. Remove any one function and the phone never reaches a customer: no operations means nothing is built, no marketing means no one knows it exists, no finance means no money to start. In large firms these are separate departments with many staff; in a tiny startup, one or two founders wear all the hats at once, but the work itself is the same.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which function turns inputs into finished goods or services? 2) Which function recruits and trains staff? 3) A firm wants to know last year's profit - which function produces that report? 4) Which function decides how to raise and invest money? 5) Which function coordinates all the others toward shared goals? Answers: 1) Operations. 2) Human resources. 3) Accounting (which prepares the reports; finance and management then use them). 4) Finance. 5) Management. Each area is a cluster of related work, and in a small firm one person may cover several of them.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing marketing with sales only. Marketing is the whole task of understanding customers and shaping the offer, not just advertising. Mistake: mixing up finance and accounting. Accounting records and reports what happened; finance looks forward and decides how to use money. Mistake: thinking small firms have no functions. They still do all the work - a few people simply cover many areas at once. Exit ticket: (a) Which function is the engine room that actually makes the product? (b) Which function produces the reports that show how the firm performed? Answers: (a) operations; (b) accounting.

questions.prompt: The core thing every surviving business must create is...
options: value a customer will pay for
questions.explanation: A business lasts only by creating value people are willing to pay for.

questions.prompt: In a sole proprietorship, the owner's liability for business debts is...
questions.explanation: There is no legal separation, so the owner is personally liable for everything.

questions.prompt: Double taxation is most associated with which form?
questions.explanation: Corporate profit can be taxed at the company level and again as dividends to owners.

questions.prompt: Which function is responsible for turning inputs into the actual product or service?
questions.explanation: Operations is the engine room that makes and delivers the output.

questions.prompt: Accounting differs from finance mainly because accounting...
options: records and reports what has already happened
questions.explanation: Accounting records and reports; finance looks forward to raising and investing money.

questions.prompt: A limited liability company is attractive because it combines...
options: limited liability with pass-through, single taxation
questions.explanation: An LLC shields owners like a corporation while profit is usually taxed only once.

lessons.title: The economic environment and markets
lessons.grammar_note: 'Supply' is how much producers will offer at a given price; 'demand' is how much buyers will purchase at that price - keep the two straight.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the economic environment a business operates in and explain how supply, demand, and competition shape prices and choices. By the end you should be able to predict, in rough terms, what happens to a price when demand rises or supply falls, and say why competition tends to push prices down and quality up. Warm-up: picture tickets for a popular concert selling out in minutes while seats for a quiet midweek show stay empty and cheap. Same kind of product, wildly different prices - what is going on? The answer lies in how many people want the thing versus how much of it is available, and that tug of war between buyers and sellers runs underneath nearly every decision a business makes about what to offer and what to charge.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A market is any place, physical or virtual, where buyers and sellers meet to trade. Two forces set the price. Demand describes how much buyers want at each price; as a rule, lower prices draw more buyers. Supply describes how much sellers will offer at each price; higher prices tempt more sellers to produce. The price tends to settle where the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers offer, called the equilibrium. When demand rises but supply holds steady, the price climbs; when supply grows while demand holds, the price falls. Competition is the number and strength of rival sellers. Where many firms compete, each must keep prices keen and quality high or lose customers; where one firm dominates, it has more power to raise prices. Businesses also sit inside a wider environment of laws, technology, interest rates, and social trends, all of which shift supply, demand, or both over time.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Return to the concert. Demand for the popular act is huge while the number of seats is fixed, so supply cannot rise to meet it; the price soars and tickets vanish. The quiet midweek show has plenty of seats and few eager buyers, so the price stays low. Weather works the same way: a frost that ruins an orange crop cuts supply, and orange juice prices jump even though demand did not change. Competition reshapes the picture too. On a street with ten coffee shops, no single shop can charge far above the others without losing customers, so prices cluster and each shop competes on quality and service. A lone shop in a remote town faces little competition and can charge more. Smart firms read these signals: they raise output or prices when demand runs ahead of supply, trim costs when rivals undercut them, and watch the wider environment for shifts in rules, rates, and tastes that move the whole market.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Demand for a toy jumps before the holidays while supply is fixed - what happens to the price? 2) A bumper harvest doubles the supply of wheat - what happens to its price? 3) Why do prices tend to cluster on a street full of competing shops? 4) What is the equilibrium price? 5) Name one wider force that can shift a whole market. Answers: 1) The price rises. 2) The price falls. 3) No shop can charge much above rivals without losing customers, so competition pulls prices together. 4) The price at which the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers offer. 5) Any of: new laws, new technology, interest rates, or changing social trends.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking a business sets prices freely. In a competitive market, buyers and rivals set tight limits on what you can charge. Mistake: confusing a change in demand with a change in supply - a frost hits supply, a holiday rush hits demand, and the two push price in different ways. Mistake: ignoring the wider environment; a rule change or a rate rise can swamp a clever pricing plan. Exit ticket: (a) If demand rises and supply stays flat, which way does price move? (b) What does strong competition tend to do to prices and quality? Answers: (a) price rises; (b) it pushes prices down and quality up.

lessons.title: How firms make money and read financial statements
lessons.grammar_note: 'Revenue' is money coming in from sales; 'profit' is what remains after costs - never use the two words as if they mean the same thing.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how a firm actually makes money and read the three basic financial statements - the income statement, the balance sheet, and the cash flow statement. By the end you should be able to compute profit from revenue and costs, tell the difference between fixed and variable costs, and say what each statement tells an owner. Warm-up: suppose a lemonade stand takes in 100 in sales over a weekend but spent 30 on lemons, sugar, and cups and 20 on the table it rented. Did it make money, and if so how much? Work it out roughly in your head before reading on, because that single subtraction is the beating heart of every business, from a stand on the pavement to a company worth billions.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Revenue is the total money a business takes in from selling its goods or services: price times quantity sold. Costs are everything the firm spends to produce and deliver that output. Fixed costs stay the same whatever the volume, such as rent; variable costs rise and fall with output, such as ingredients. Profit is revenue minus total costs - what is left over, and the reward that keeps owners and the firm going. To track all this, firms use three statements. The income statement shows revenue, costs, and the resulting profit over a period, answering 'did we make money?' The balance sheet is a snapshot at one moment of what the firm owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities), and the owners' share (equity), where assets always equal liabilities plus equity. The cash flow statement tracks cash moving in and out, because a profitable firm can still run out of cash if money is tied up or bills come due early.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Take the lemonade stand. Revenue is 100. Variable costs are 30 for lemons, sugar, and cups; the fixed cost is 20 for the table. Total cost is 50, so profit is 100 minus 50, which is 50. The income statement would list revenue 100, costs 50, profit 50. Now suppose the stand owns a jug and a cooler worth 40 and owes a friend 10 it borrowed for supplies; its balance sheet shows assets of 40 plus whatever cash it holds, a liability of 10, and the rest as the owner's equity, with the two sides always equal. The cash flow statement would show the 100 coming in and the 50 going out, leaving 50 in cash. Scale this up and the logic holds: a large firm just has more line items. Watching the gap between revenue and costs, and keeping enough cash on hand, is how any business survives and grows.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) A shop has revenue of 500 and total costs of 380 - what is its profit? 2) Is rent a fixed or a variable cost? 3) Which statement tells you what a firm owns and owes at a single moment? 4) Can a profitable firm still run short of cash? 5) Write the balance sheet equation. Answers: 1) 500 minus 380 equals 120. 2) Fixed - it does not change with how much you sell. 3) The balance sheet. 4) Yes - profit can be locked up in unpaid invoices or stock while bills come due, which is why cash flow matters. 5) Assets equal liabilities plus equity.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating revenue as profit. High sales mean nothing if costs are higher; only the difference counts. Mistake: calling every cost fixed. Variable costs move with output, and mixing the two wrecks any forecast. Mistake: assuming profit equals cash in the bank. A firm can be profitable on paper yet unable to pay its bills if the cash has not arrived. Exit ticket: (a) Give the formula for profit. (b) Which statement would you read to see whether a firm has enough cash to pay its bills? Answers: (a) profit equals revenue minus total costs; (b) the cash flow statement.

lessons.title: Marketing, the customer, and the supply chain
lessons.grammar_note: The 'supply chain' is the whole sequence from raw materials to the finished product in a customer's hands, not just the delivery van at the end.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how marketing puts the customer at the center of a business and how operations and the supply chain actually deliver on the promise marketing makes. By the end you should be able to describe the four classic marketing levers - product, price, place, and promotion - and trace a product backward from the shelf to its raw materials. Warm-up: pick any item near you and ask two questions. First, how did you come to want it - what told you it existed and that it was worth the price? Second, how did it physically get to you, step by step, from wherever its parts began? The first question is marketing; the second is operations and the supply chain, and a healthy business has to answer both well at the same time.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Marketing begins with the customer: it studies what people need, then shapes an offer they will value. A classic way to organize marketing is the four levers, often called the marketing mix: product, the thing itself and how well it fits the need; price, what to charge given value and competition; place, where and how customers can buy it; and promotion, how the firm makes the offer known, from advertising to word of mouth. Marketing identifies the target customer and aims these levers at them. Operations and the supply chain then keep the promise. Operations makes or assembles the product and manages quality and timing. The supply chain is the full network that carries goods from raw materials through suppliers, factories, and warehouses to the final buyer. When marketing promises fast, reliable delivery, the supply chain has to deliver it; when it fails, the brand suffers no matter how clever the advertising.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Think about a running shoe. Marketing researches runners, designs a shoe for them (product), sets a price that signals quality without scaring buyers off (price), sells it both in stores and online (place), and runs ads and sponsorships to build desire (promotion). Now trace the supply chain backward: the shoe on the shelf came from a warehouse, which received it from a factory, which assembled rubber, foam, and fabric sourced from several suppliers, who in turn drew on raw materials like latex and cotton. A delay or fault anywhere in that chain - a strike at a port, a shortage of foam - can empty the shelves even when demand is strong. Good firms coordinate the two sides: marketing does not promise next-day delivery the supply chain cannot meet, and operations flags shortages early so marketing can manage expectations. The customer at the end sees one smooth experience, but behind it sit dozens of linked steps that all have to work.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the four levers of the marketing mix. 2) Which lever covers where customers can buy the product? 3) What is a supply chain, in one sentence? 4) Give one event that could disrupt a supply chain. 5) Why must marketing and operations coordinate their promises? Answers: 1) Product, price, place, and promotion. 2) Place. 3) The full network that carries goods from raw materials, through suppliers and factories, to the final customer. 4) Any of: a port strike, a material shortage, a factory breakdown, or a transport delay. 5) Because marketing sets customer expectations that operations and the supply chain must actually be able to meet.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking marketing is only advertising. Promotion is just one of four levers; product, price, and place matter as much or more. Mistake: treating the supply chain as only the last delivery step. It stretches all the way back to raw materials. Mistake: letting marketing promise what operations cannot deliver, which breaks customer trust. Exit ticket: (a) Which marketing lever is about making the offer known? (b) Why can a supply chain problem hurt a firm even when demand is strong? Answers: (a) promotion; (b) if goods cannot be made or moved, shelves go empty and customers cannot buy no matter how much they want to.

lessons.title: Ethics, responsibility, entrepreneurship, and the global context
lessons.grammar_note: 'Ethics' is about what is right to do; 'law' is about what you are required to do - an action can be legal yet still unethical.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain business ethics and corporate social responsibility, describe how an entrepreneur turns an idea into a venture through a business plan, and place a firm in its global, many-stakeholder context. By the end you should be able to tell ethics apart from mere law, list the main parts of a business plan, and name the groups a global firm must answer to. Warm-up: imagine a factory that can cut costs by dumping waste into a river where no rule yet forbids it. It would be legal and more profitable - so should the firm do it? Sit with that question, because it marks the line between what a business can do and what it should do, and that line runs through every topic in this final lesson, from responsibility to the global reach of modern firms.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Business ethics is the study of what is right and wrong in how a firm acts, going beyond what the law strictly requires. Corporate social responsibility, often written as corporate social responsibility or CSR, is a firm taking ownership of its wider effect on people and the planet, from fair wages to a smaller footprint. Both rest on the stakeholder view: a business answers not only to its owners but to customers, workers, suppliers, communities, and future generations. Entrepreneurship is the act of spotting an opportunity and building a venture to pursue it, accepting risk in the hope of reward. The main tool is the business plan, a written case that sets out the idea, the target market, the operations, the team, and the financial forecast before real money is risked. Finally, modern firms are global: they buy, sell, and hire across borders, which widens both their opportunities and their responsibilities to many more stakeholders at once.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Return to the factory by the river. Dumping waste may be legal today, but an ethical firm weighs the harm to the community and the environment and declines, perhaps investing in cleaner methods instead - that choice is corporate social responsibility in action, and it often protects the brand and keeps regulators and neighbors on side. Now picture an entrepreneur who notices that local bakeries throw away unsold bread each night. She drafts a business plan: the idea is an app and service that sells surplus bread cheaply at closing time; the market is price-conscious shoppers and bakeries wanting less waste; operations covers pickups and payments; the forecast shows when revenue would cover costs. The plan lets her test the idea on paper and persuade a lender before risking savings. Scale her venture up and it becomes global - sourcing, selling, and hiring in many countries - and now she answers to stakeholders worldwide, from overseas workers to distant communities, which makes ethics and responsibility larger, not smaller.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) How does ethics differ from law? 2) What does corporate social responsibility mean, in one sentence? 3) Name three parts of a business plan. 4) What does an entrepreneur accept in the hope of reward? 5) Why does going global widen a firm's responsibilities? Answers: 1) Law is what you must do; ethics is what is right to do, and an action can be legal yet still unethical. 2) A firm taking responsibility for its wider impact on people and the planet, not only its profit. 3) Any three of: the idea, the target market, operations, the team, and the financial forecast. 4) Risk - including the chance of losing the money and effort invested. 5) It adds many more stakeholders across borders, from overseas workers to distant communities and environments.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming that legal always means ethical. The two often agree, but not always, and the gap is where reputations are made or lost. Mistake: treating corporate social responsibility as mere advertising. Done well, it changes real behavior, not just slogans. Mistake: thinking a business plan guarantees success. It reduces risk by forcing hard thinking, but customers and markets still decide. Exit ticket: (a) Can an action be legal yet unethical? (b) Name two stakeholders a global firm must consider beyond its owners. Answers: (a) yes - legality and ethics are not the same; (b) any two of customers, employees, suppliers, communities, and the environment.
